perly, not necessarily go before, and after it. I say, properly, but not necessarily in such a Sense, that the Communion would be no Communion without it; but suitably to the good Design and Tendency of this Rite, and most usefully to ourselves. And again,
'Tis always to be remember'd, that every Petition or Thanksgiving used in the publick Office [that of the Church of England] throughout our whole Attendance upon this Duty, is not a part of the Duty itself, which (strictly taken) is comprehended within the Limits of eating and drinking with a due Remembrance of Christ's Death.
FARTHER, the Duty (that of receiving the Sacrament) ought always to be consider'd as distinct from all Expressions, Prayers or Thanksgivings, which are made use of before and after it.
This Doctrine you profess to draw from the Holy Scriptures, and them alone; and you declare in the very Title-Page of your Book, that your whole Doctrine about the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper is drawn from Texts in the New Testament, and them alone.

I propose farther to shew, that the Scriptures require antecedent moral Dispositions or Behaviour, as Qualifications in the Receiver of this Sacrament, in order to his receiving the blessed Sacrament acceptably to God; and particularly hope to make it appear, that St. Paul requires such Qualifications in that very Passage to the Corinthians, from which you have labour'd to reject all antecedent Preparation, but that of our own Hearts and Dispositions by the Institution of this holy Rite, in order to assure ourselves we will go to the Lord's Supper, and behave at it, not as a common Meal.

AND acceptably to God, &c.
Now, not to stay to consider whether if this is what you assert, we might not comply with Christ's whole Design, if we did not eat and drink at all; we grant that, if all that Christ requires, if his whole Design, as it relates to our Practice in this Ordinance, is the Remembrance of himself; then it must follow, that whoever performs the Actions of eating and drinking suitably to this Design, must perform them acceptably to God, &c.
But how does it appear from these Passages, that this is Christ's whole Design with regard to our Practice? Or that antecedent moral Dispositions or Behaviour are not required as Qualifications in the Receiver of his Sacrament, in order to his receiving it acceptably to God, &c.

blocks.text: For this Crime he reproves them severely, ver. 22. thus: Have ye not Houses of your own for your ordinary eating and drinking? Or have you no Sense, that these Assemblies of Christians come together for the religious Purpose of eating and drinking in remembrance of their Master, and that the Place where they meet for this good End is not the proper Place for your ordinary Meals, much less for your Excesses in drinking? Do ye thus despise the Church of God, the Assemblies of Christians, and the Place you at this time profess to meet in for religious; and not for common Purposes, and thus put to shame those of your poor Brethren who are not able to make Provision for themselves, by such a Behaviour as seems to insult their Poverty and Hunger in such publick Meetings? From the Nature and End of the Institution of the Lord's Supper; (here set forth) it follows, that every one who comes to this Table of the Lord, and instead of behaving himself worthily, that is, suitable to the good End of this Holy Rite; and instead of a serious performance of the Actions of eating and drinking in Remembrance of Christ his Master, eats and drinks unworthily, or in a manner unsuitable to the Design of this Institution; behaving himself as at a common Meal, or, as if this was only the Continuation of a foregoing Entertainment, and even without observing the Rules of Temperance; every such profess'd Christian is guilty of a very high Offence and Indignity against the very Body and Blood of Christ, of which this Bread and this Wine are Memorials; and which he pretends and professes to remember, by this eating and drinking.

blocks.text: Ver. 29. I say, let a Man try and approve himself, and perform this Part of his religious Duty suitably to the Design of it, the Remembrance of Christ; because great will be his Offence if he wilfully performs it in a contrary Way; or, in a manner plainly unworthy of the Institution. For, he that eateth and drinketh as some of you have done, unworthily, that is, unsuitably to that Design, and in a manner utterly inconsistent with it; not discerning the Lord's Body, that is, not considering this Bread as the Memorial of his Body; not making sufficient Difference between this Bread eaten at the Lord's Supper, in Memory of him, and a common Meal, even intemperately taken: He that eats thus, eats and drinks Damnation, Condemnation or Judgment to himself, whilst he professes and pretends to meet his Fellow Christians at the Lord's Table, and at the same time behaves himself as at no other than a common Meal; nay, even with Intemperance and Indecency: and by this lays himself justly open to the Displeasure of Almighty God. blocks.text: Allowing that the Crime for which St. Paul reproves the Corinthians, is an indecent manner of eating and drinking; that this is what he tells them is eating and drinking unworthily; yet it does not at all follow, that none need be affrighted at the Words of St. Paul, but those who eat and drink in a sinful indecent manner. And if certain antecedent moral Dispositions or Behaviour should be required as Qualifications in the Receiver of this Sacrament, in order to his receiving it acceptably to God, &c. then those Persons who come to the Table of the Lord without such Qualifications, will have reason to be affrighted at these Words of St. Paul, tho' they were not directly spoken to them; and they may justly fear, that if Condemnation is pronounc'd for only eating and drinking in an improper manner, that a greater Condemnation will be pronounc'd for presuming to come to the Table of the Lord without those Qualifications.

These Propositions all follow, if the Sacrament is consider'd as a human Institution; and the Old Testament will appear to be excluded from delivering any thing which can lead us to a Knowledge of the Nature and Extent of this particular Duty.

For where should we find the Will of an Institutor but in his Words?

Or how can we expect to find the Will of a Person where his Will is not declar'd?

And then also would the 8th Proposition be allow'd to follow, tho' in that Proposition it should be asserted, that the End which Christ proposed should be obtain'd by this Duty was the Remembrance of himself: for every Body knows so much of the human Mind, as to know that the Pleasure of being remember'd is a great Motive of human Actions.

Thus the Reader sees upon these Premises that Jesus as a Man, and independently of God, instituted this Sacrament, the Old Testament will be excluded, as not delivering any thing which can lead us to a Knowledge of the Nature and Extent of this Duty, or the Will of the Institutor of this positive Institution call'd the Sacrament.

blocks.text: Now then, as in order to your Conclusion, the Old Testament, and all other Parts of the New, besides those which have been paraphras'd, must be excluded from delivering any thing which can lead us to a Knowledge of the Nature and Extent of this religious Duty, or the Will of God as it relates to this Sacrament; and as no Evidence is given why the Old Testament should be excluded from doing this; and as no Premises appear by which it will be excluded from doing it, unless it were supposed in the first Proposition, that Jesus, independently of God, instituted this Duty; and as no Evidence is given by which all other Parts of the New Testament, besides the Texts which have been paraphras'd, will be excluded from doing this, unless it be bare Assertion; it is not yet proved that what is found necessary in the Texts which are paraphras'd, in order to our performing this Duty acceptably to God, &c. in all that is necessary in order to this End; and antecedent moral Dispositions or Behaviour may be required as Qualifications in the Receiver of this Sacrament, for any thing which has hitherto appear'd to the contrary.
